questions.q: Why are log returns often preferred for statistical calculations like means and variances?
options: They are always larger in magnitude than simple returns
They add across time periods instead of compounding multiplicatively, which is more convenient for statistics
They are what actually determines your account balance
Regulators require log returns for all performance reporting
questions.explain: Log returns sum across periods (total log return = sum of period log returns), which makes them convenient for statistical work, while simple returns compound multiplicatively and are what determines actual account balance.

questions.q: When annualizing daily volatility, why is it conventionally scaled by the square root of 252 rather than 252 itself?
options: There is no mathematical reason, it is purely a convention with no basis
Because volatility (standard deviation) scales with the square root of time under the assumption of roughly independent daily returns
Because returns are scaled by 252 and volatility must match that exactly
Because 252 trading days per year is itself an estimate
questions.explain: Under the square-root-of-time rule, variance scales linearly with time (for independent returns), so standard deviation (volatility) scales with the square root of time — hence sqrt(252) for daily-to-annual conversion.

questions.q: What is the key difference between the Sharpe ratio and the Sortino ratio?
options: Sharpe uses annual data while Sortino uses daily data
Sortino ignores risk entirely, while Sharpe accounts for it
Sharpe penalizes both upside and downside volatility equally; Sortino only penalizes downside volatility (below a target)
They are two names for the exact same calculation
questions.explain: The Sharpe ratio divides excess return by total volatility, treating upside and downside swings the same. The Sortino ratio instead divides by downside deviation, computed only from returns below a target threshold, so it doesn't penalize upside volatility.

questions.q: A strategy has small, frequent losses and rare, large gains (classic trend-following shape). What would you expect to see when comparing its Sharpe and Sortino ratios?
options: Sharpe and Sortino would be identical, since the ratios always match
Sortino would be noticeably higher than Sharpe, since total volatility is inflated by the large upside moves that Sortino ignores
Sortino would be noticeably lower than Sharpe
Neither ratio can be computed for asymmetric return patterns
questions.explain: Because Sortino only counts downside deviation, and this strategy's large moves are upside (gains), its total volatility (used by Sharpe) is inflated by moves that Sortino doesn't penalize at all — so Sortino comes out higher.

questions.q: What is the lesson's warning about treating a single Sharpe ratio from one backtest run as a trustworthy verdict?
options: Sharpe ratios are never useful and should not be computed
A single point estimate from a short run has real estimation error, and a Sharpe that was itself the selection criterion in a parameter search is not a trustworthy future estimate
Sharpe ratios are only valid for ratios above 3.0
Sharpe ratios should never be annualized
questions.explain: The lesson ties this back to Chapter 4's overfitting warning: a Sharpe ratio chosen because it was the best result of a search is biased upward, and even an honestly-computed one carries real sampling error over a short period — Lesson 25 quantifies this further.
